Umar ibn al-Khattab said to him, "Do not burden the Prophet ﷺ." He said: "Leave him, O son of al-Khattab." He said: So this surah was revealed to him while the man was with him. When he recited it to him and reached the description of the Gardens, the man let out a sigh, and his soul departed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The longing for Paradise has taken the soul of your companion, or your brother." It is also narrated from Ibn Umar with a different wording, which will come later. Al-Qushayri said: This surah was revealed concerning Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. However, the purpose of the surah is general, and the same applies to everything that is said to have been revealed for such-and-such a reason.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning? Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture, to test him; and We made him hearing and seeing. Indeed, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful.﴾

His saying, ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ "Hal" here means "qad" (indeed/already), as said by al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Abu Ubayda. It has also been reported from Sibawayh that "hal" means "qad."

Al-Farra' said: "Hal" can be a negation and can be an affirmation. This one is affirmative, because you say, "Have I not given you?" meaning you are confirming that you gave it. Negation is when you say, "Can anyone do the like of this?" It was also said that it has the force of an interrogative, and the meaning is "has come" (atā).

"Man" here refers to Adam, peace be upon him, as said by Qatada, al-Thawri, Ikrima and al-Suddi, and it is also reported from Ibn Abbas.

"A period of time": Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Abu Salih, said: Forty years passed over him before the spirit was breathed into him, while he was lying between Mecca and al-Ta'if. Also from Ibn Abbas, in the narration of al-Dahhak, that he was created from clay, and remained for forty years; then from black mud shaped (hama' masnun) for forty years; then from dried clay (salsal) for forty years; so his creation was completed after one hundred and twenty years. Ibn Mas'ud added, saying: He remained for forty years made of dust, so his creation was completed after one hundred and sixty years, and then the spirit was breathed into him.

It was also said that the "period" mentioned here is not known in its duration, also from Ibn Abbas, related by al-Mawardi.

﴿A thing worth mentioning﴾: al-Dahhak reported from Ibn Abbas: neither in the heaven nor on the earth. It was also said: That is, he was a shaped body of dust and clay, not mentioned, not known, and it was not known what his name was or what was intended by him. Then the spirit was breathed into him, and he became worth mentioning. This was said by al-Farra', Qutrub and Tha'lab. Yahya ibn Salam said: He was not a thing worth mentioning among creation, even though he was a thing worth mentioning with Allah.

It was also said: This "mention" is not in the sense of information, since the Lord's informing about existents is eternal; rather, this mention means prominence, nobility and rank. You say, "So-and-so is mentioned," meaning he has nobility and rank. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44], meaning: there came upon man a period when he had no rank among creation. Then, when Allah informed the angels that He would make Adam a khalifa (vicegerent), and entrusted him with the trust which the heavens, the earth and the mountains refused to bear, his excellence over all became manifest, and so he became worth mentioning.

Al-Qushayri said: In general, he was not mentioned by creation, even though he was mentioned by Allah.

Muhammad ibn al-Jahm related from al-Farra': "He was not a thing," and then said: "He was a thing, but was not worth mentioning."

Some people said: The negation refers to the thing itself. That is: periods of time had passed while Adam was not a thing worth mentioning among creation, because he was the last of the kinds of creation that He created, and what does not exist is not a thing until a period comes upon it. The meaning is: times passed over him while Adam was neither a thing, nor created, nor mentioned by anyone of creation. This is the meaning of the saying of Qatada and Muqatil. Qatada said: Man was created recently, as far as we know of the creation of Allah, may His praise be exalted, a creation that came after man. Muqatil said: There is inversion (taqdim and ta'khir) in the speech, and its sense is: "Has there come upon man a period of time when man was not a thing worth mentioning?", because He created him after the creation of all living beings, and He did not create any living being after him.

It has also been said: "Man" in His saying ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time﴾ is meant as the species (jins) of Adam's descendants, and that the "period" is nine months, the duration of a human being's gestation in its mother's womb, during which he was not a thing worth mentioning, for he was then a clinging clot and a lump of flesh, being in that state an inanimate thing with no rank.

Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, when he recited this verse, said: "Would that it had been completed, so that we would not be tested." That is, would that the period which passed over Adam had been completed in that state, so that he would not have begotten and his offspring would not be tested.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, heard a man reciting ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ and said: "Would that it had been completed."

﴿Indeed, We created man﴾: that is, the son of Adam, without any disagreement, ﴿from a sperm-drop﴾: that is, from water that drips, which is the semen. Every small amount of water in a vessel is a *nutfah*, as in the saying of Abdullah ibn Rawaha rebuking himself:

"What is it with me that I see you hating Paradise?
Are you not but a drop in a waterskin?"

Its plural is *nutaf* and *nitaf*.

*Amshaj*: mixtures. Its singular is *mishj* and *mashij*, like *khidn* and *khadin*. Ru'ba said:

"They cast off every hurried, lively one
Who had not been clothed with skin in mixed blood."

It is said: "I mixed this with that" (mashaja), that is, I blended it, so it is *mamshuj* and *mashij*, like *makhlut* and *khalit*. Al-Mubarrad said: The singular of *amshaj* is *mashij*; one says *mashaja yamshiju* when he mixes, and here it means the mixing of the sperm-drop with blood. Al-Shammakh said:

"The inner parts of one trembling for a moment folded
Over a mixture whose lineage is despised."

Al-Farra' said: *Amshaj* are mixtures of the man's water and the woman's water, and blood and the clot. What is mixed of these is called *mashij*, as you say *khalij*, and *mamshuj*, as you say *makhlut*.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: *Amshaj* means redness in whiteness, and whiteness in redness. This is an opinion preferred by many of the lexicographers. Al-Hudhali [[This is Amr ibn al-Dakhil al-Hudhali. In (Lisan al-Arab: mashaja) it is attributed to Zuhayr ibn Haram al-Hudhali. "Sit bihi" means: there came out feathers mixed with blood and water.]] said:

"As if the feathers and the two ends of it,
Opposite the arrowhead, were smeared with mashij."

It is also from Ibn Abbas that he said: The man's water, which is white and thick, mixes with the woman's water, which is yellow and thin, and from both the child is created. Whatever is of sinew, bone and strength is from the man's water, and whatever is of flesh, blood and hair is from the woman's water. This has been reported as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet ﷺ) narration, mentioned by al-Bazzar.

It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: *amshajuha* are the veins of the lump of flesh. And from him: the water of the man and the water of the woman, and they are two colours. Mujahid said: The man's sperm-drop is white and red, and the woman's sperm-drop is green and yellow. Ibn Abbas said: He was created from various colours: created from dust, then from the water of the womb and the uterus, and it is a sperm-drop, then a clot, then a lump, then bone, then flesh. Qatada said something similar: they are stages of creation: a stage, and another stage; a clot, and a lump, then bones, then He clothes the bones with flesh, as He said in the surah "al-Mu'minun": ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12], to the end of the verse.

Ibn al-Sikkit said: *Amshaj* are mixtures, because they are blended from kinds, so man was created from them with diverse natures.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: *Amshaj* is what is collected, and it has the sense of the singular, because it is an adjective of *nutfah*, as one says: *burmah a'shar* (a pot that is in pieces) and *thawb akhlaq* (a worn-out garment).

It is reported from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari that he said: A Jewish rabbi came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Tell me about the water of the man and the water of the woman?" He said: [The man's water is white and thick, and the woman's water is yellow and thin. If the woman's water prevails, she bears a female; and if the man's water prevails, he causes a male to be born.] The rabbi said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that you are the Messenger of Allah."

This opinion has already been discussed fully in surah "al-Baqarah."

﴿To test him﴾: that is, to examine him. It was also said: We ordain a test for him, and a test is an examination. As for what he is tested by, there are two views. The first: We test him with good and evil, said al-Kalbi. The second: We test his gratitude in ease and his patience in hardship, said al-Hasan.

It was also said: "We test him" means: We impose obligations on him. Here too there are two views. The first: by acting after creation, said Muqatil. The second: by religion, so that he may be commanded to obey and forbidden from sins.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas: "We test him": We turn him from creation to creation, so that We may test him with good and evil. Muhammad ibn al-Jahm related from al-Farra', who said: The meaning, and Allah knows best, is: ﴿and We made him hearing and seeing﴾ in order to test him. And this is a case of anticipation whose meaning is delay. [[Note from the author: because testing only occurs after the completion of the creation.]]

It was also said: ﴿We made him hearing and seeing﴾: meaning, We gave him hearing by which he hears guidance, and sight by which he sees guidance.

﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾: that is, We made clear to him and made known to him the path of guidance and misguidance, and good and evil, by sending the Messengers. So he believed or disbelieved, as in His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. Mujahid said: That is, We made clear to him the way to wretchedness and to felicity. Al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and al-Suddi said: "The way" here is his coming out from the womb. It was also said: His benefits and harms by which he is guided through his natural disposition and the perfection of his intellect.

(إِمَّا شاكِراً وَإِمَّا كَفُوراً) — that is, whichever of the two they choose, We have already made the way clear to him. The Kufans said: here "in" (inna) functions as a conditional particle and "ma" is superfluous, meaning: We made the way clear to him, whether he gives thanks or disbelieves. Al-Farra' preferred this view, but the Basrians did not permit it, since the conditional "in" does not enter upon nouns unless a verb is understood after it.

It has also been said: the meaning is "We guided him to the right path," that is, We made clear to him the way of monotheism by setting up the proofs for it; then, if We create guidance in him, he is guided and believes, and if We forsake him, he disbelieves. This is like your saying: "I have advised you; if you wish, accept, and if you wish, leave it," meaning "if you wish," with the fa' (fa) omitted. Likewise is "whether grateful" (imma shakiran), and Allah knows best.

It is said: "hadaytuhu al-sabil," "hadaytuhu lil-sabil," and "hadaytuhu ila al-sabil." This has been discussed earlier in al-Fatiha [see vol. 1, pp. 147 and 160] and elsewhere.

He combined "shakir" (grateful) with "kafur" (ungrateful), and did not combine "shakur" (very grateful) with "kafur," even though both share the sense of intensification. This negates intensity in gratitude and affirms it in disbelief, because the gratitude owed to Allah the Exalted cannot be fully rendered, so intensity is withheld from it, whereas intensity is not withheld from disbelief; so his gratitude is little, due to the abundance of blessings upon him, while his disbelief is abundant, even if it is little, given the kindness shown to him. This was related by al-Mawardi.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 76, verse 4:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains, shackles, and a blazing Fire.﴾ He explains the condition of the two groups. He imposed worship on rational beings, obligated them, and enabled them to do what He commanded them. Whoever disbelieves has punishment, and whoever affirms God's oneness and gives thanks has reward. *Al-salasil* (the chains) are the fetters in Hell. The length of each chain is seventy cubits, as has passed in *al-Haqqah* [[See vol. 18, p. 272.]].

Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr (on the authority of 'Asim) and Hisham (on the authority of Ibn 'Amir) read *salasila* with tanwin (nunation). The rest read it without tanwin. Qunbul, Ibn Kathir, and Hamza pause on it without an alif. The rest pause with the alif.

As for the first *qawarir*, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr (on the authority of 'Asim) read it with tanwin, and the rest do not. Ya'qub and Hamza pause on it without an alif, and the rest pause with the alif. As for the second *qawarir*, Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr also read it with tanwin, and the rest do not. Whoever reads with tanwin reads it with the alif, and whoever does not read with tanwin drops the alif from it.

Abu 'Ubayd preferred tanwin in all three words, and pausing with the alif, following the script of the Mushaf. He said: "I saw in the Mushaf of 'Uthman *salasila* with an alif, and *qawariraa*, the first with an alif. The second was written with an alif, but it was scraped out, and I saw its trace there clearly."

Whoever reads with tanwin has four arguments. The first: plural forms resembled singular forms, so they were treated as singular nouns and given the rules of singulars, and therefore they take tanwin. The second: al-Akhfash reported from the Arabs the inflection with tanwin of all words that are normally not inflected, except *af'alu minka* (the comparative form). Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said likewise that this follows the dialect of those who put all nouns in the genitive case, except in their saying *huwa atrafu minka* (he is more refined than you), for they do not put it in the genitive. Ibn al-Anbari cited in this regard the verse of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

*Our swords among us and among them are like balls* ... *in the hands of our players*

Labid said:

*And a camel slaughtered for gambling, whose fate I called for* ... *with arrows whose bodies are alike*

Labid also said:

*Generous, and one who helps in generosity, gracious, bountiful, whose flock of gifts is abundant*

So he inflected *makharik*, *maghaliq*, and *raghaib* with tanwin, though the proper course is that they should not be inflected.

The third argument: the first *qawarir* was given tanwin because it is the end of a verse (*ra's al-aya*), and verse-ends came with nunation, as in His saying: ﴿*mudhkuran*﴾ and ﴿*sami'an basiran*﴾. So they gave the first word tanwin so that a pause could be made between verse-ends, and they gave the second word tanwin by analogy with the first.

The fourth argument: following the copies of the Mushaf, for both words are written with an alif in the copies of Makkah, Madinah, and Kufa.

Those who did not inflect these words argued: every plural form that has after its alif three letters, or two letters, or a doubled letter, is not inflected, whether definite or indefinite. What has three letters after its alif is like your saying *qanadil*, *dananeer*, and *manadil*. What has two letters after its alif is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿*lahudimat sawami'*﴾ [22:40], because after its alif there are two letters. Likewise His saying: ﴿*wa masajidu yudhkaru fiha ismu Allahi kathira*﴾ [22:40]. What has a doubled letter after its alif is *shawabb* and *dawabb*.

Khalaf said: "I heard Yahya ibn Adam relate from Ibn Idris, who said: 'In the early copies, the first letter has an alif and the second has no alif.'" This is an argument for the position of Hamza. Khalaf also said: "I saw in a copy attributed to the reading of Ibn Mas'ud that the first has an alif and the second has no alif."

As for *af'alu minka*, no Arab, in poetry or otherwise, says *huwa af'alu minka* with tanwin, because *min* stands in place of the annexation (*idafa*). So tanwin and annexation are not combined in one word, since they are two indicators of nouns, and two indicators are not combined. This was said by al-Farra' and others.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿*wa aghlalan*﴾ (and shackles). It is the plural of *ghull*, by which their hands are fettered to their necks.

It is reported from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda', that he used to say: "Raise these hands to God, may His praise be great, before they are shackled with the shackles." Al-Hasan said: "The shackles are not placed on the necks of the people of the Fire because they have made the Lord, glorified is He, incapable, but as a humiliation."

As for ﴿*sa'iran*﴾ (a blazing Fire), its discussion has already passed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 76, verse 5–6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous (al-abrar) will drink from a cup﴾. Al-abrar: the people of truthfulness. Its singular is barr, and it is one who complies with the command of God, exalted is He. It was said: al-barr is the monotheist (al-muwahhid), and al-abrar is the plural of barr (bārr), like shahid and ashhad. It was said: it is the plural of barr, like nahr and anhar. In al-Sihah: the plural of al-barr is al-abrar, and the plural of al-barr (bārr) is al-barara. One says: so-and-so yabarru his Creator and yatabarraruh, meaning he obeys Him; and the mother is barra (dutiful) toward her child.

Ibn Umar narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: [God, exalted is His praise, named them al-abrar only because they were dutiful to fathers and sons, just as your father has a right over you, so too your son has a right over you.] Al-Hasan said: the barr is the one who does not harm an ant. Qatadah said: the abrar are those who fulfil God's right and keep their vows. And in a hadith: [The abrar are those who do not harm anyone.]

﴿Will drink from a cup﴾, i.e., from a vessel containing the drink. Ibn Abbas said: he means wine. In the language, al-ka's is the vessel containing the drink; if it contains no drink it is not called a cup. Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*Sabanta al-ka's 'anna umma 'Amrin...* [[The well-known narration in the Mu'allaqat: sadadta al-ka's.]] — *wa kana al-ka's majraha al-yaminā*

Al-Asma'i said: it is said *sabanta 'anna al-hadiyyata* or what is of goodness, *tasbinu sabnan*, meaning you withheld (kafaftа), as al-Jawhari said. ﴿Its mizaj﴾, i.e., its mixture and blend. Hassan said:

*Ka-anna sabi'atan min bayti Ra's* [[al-Sabi'a: wine, so named because it is bought to be drunk; in one version: "ka-anna khabi'a", meaning the guarded one, cherished for its preciousness. Bayt Ra's: a well-known place in Jordan famous for wine.]] — *yakunu mizajaha 'asalun wa ma'un*

From this is the mizaj of the body, which is what mixes with it of yellow bile, black bile, heat and cold. ﴿Kafura﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it is the name of a spring of water in Paradise, called the spring of kafur, meaning its water is mixed with this spring which is called kafur. Sa'id reported from Qatadah: it is mixed for them with kafur and sealed with musk. Mujahid also said this. Ikrimah said: its mizaj is its taste. It was said: the kafur is only in its scent, not in its taste. It was said: he meant "like kafur" in its whiteness, fragrance and coolness, because kafur is not drunk, as in His saying: ﴿until, when He made it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], i.e., like fire. Ibn Kaysan said: it is scented with musk, kafur and ginger. Muqatil said: it is not the kafur of this world, but God named what is there by what is here so that hearts may be guided to it. His saying: ﴿kana mizajuha﴾, where kana is redundant, i.e., from a cup whose mizaj is kafur.

﴿A spring from which the servants of God drink﴾. Al-Farra' said: kafur is the name of a spring of water in Paradise, so ʿaynan is a substitute (badal) for kafur on this view. It was said: it is a substitute for ka's according to its position. It was said: it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in mizajuha. It was said: it is put in the accusative by way of praise, as when a man is mentioned and you say: "the intelligent, the discerning", i.e., you mentioned the intelligent, the discerning, so it is in the accusative by an implied "I mean." It was said: they drink a spring. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "from a spring." It is said: kafur and qafur. Al-Kafur is also the sheath of the date-palm spathe, and likewise al-kufarra, as al-Asma'i said. As for the verse of al-Ra'i:

*Taksu al-mafariqa wa al-labbata dha 'arajin...* min qusbin mu'tali fa al-kafuri darraj

the gazelle from which musk comes grazes on the spikenard, so he called it kafur.

﴿Yashrabu biha﴾. Al-Farra' said: yashrabu biha and yashrabuha are the same in meaning, and yashrabu biha may be narrated as biha and yunqa'. He recited:

*Sharibna bi-ma'i al-bahri thumma tarraffa'at... mata lujajin khudrin lahunna na'ij*

He said: similarly, so-and-so speaks with good speech, and speaks good speech. It was said: the meaning is yashrabuha, and the ba' is redundant. It was said: the ba' is a substitute for, its estimated form being yashrabu minha, as al-Qutabi said.

﴿They make it gush forth in abundant flow﴾. It is said that a man among them walks in his mansions and climbs to his palaces, with a staff in his hand, pointing with it to the water, and it flows with him wherever he turns in his dwellings on ground level without a trench, and follows him wherever he climbs to the top of his palaces. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿a spring from which the servants of God drink; they make it gush forth in abundant flow﴾, i.e., they split it open, as a man makes a river flow here and there wherever he wishes. From Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿they make it gush forth in abundant flow﴾ means they lead it wherever they wish, and it follows them, wherever they turn it turns with them. Abu Muqatil narrated from Abu Salih, from Sa'd, from Abu Sahl, from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: [There are four springs in Paradise: two flow from beneath the Throne, one of which is the one God mentioned, ﴿they make it gush forth in abundant flow﴾, and the other is ginger; the other two are gushing from above the Throne, one of which is the one God mentioned, ﴿a spring therein called Salsabil﴾, and the other is Tasnim.] Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned this in Nawadir al-Usul, and said: Tasnim is for the muqarrabun exclusively as their drink, and kafur is for the abrar as their drink, mixed for the abrar from Tasnim as their beverage. As for ginger and Salsabil, the abrar have a mizaj from them; thus he mentioned this in the revelation, and was silent about who drinks it neat. So what is a mizaj for the abrar is pure for the muqarrabun, and what is pure for the abrar is a mizaj for the rest of the people of Paradise. The abrar are the truthful, and the muqarrabun are the siddiqun.

It was said: the kafur is only in its scent, not in its taste. It was said: he meant "like kafur" in its whiteness, fragrance and coolness, because kafur is not drunk, as in His saying: ﴿until, when He made it fire﴾ [al-Kahf: 96], i.e., like fire. the gazelle from which musk comes grazes on the spikenard, so he called it kafur.

﴿Yashrabu biha﴾. Al-Farra' said: yashrabu biha and yashrabuha are the same in meaning, and yashrabu biha may be narrated as biha and yunqa'. He recited:

*Sharibna bi-ma'i al-bahri thumma tarraffa'at... mata lujajin khudrin lahunna na'ij*

He said: similarly, so-and-so speaks with good speech, and speaks good speech. It was said: the meaning is yashrabuha, and the ba' is redundant. It was said: the ba' is a substitute for, its estimated form being yashrabu minha, as al-Qutabi said.

﴿They make it gush forth in abundant flow﴾. So what is a mizaj for the abrar is pure for the muqarrabun, and what is pure for the abrar is a mizaj for the rest of the people of Paradise. The abrar are the truthful, and the muqarrabun are the siddiqun.

I say: the correct view is that it was revealed concerning all the righteous and whoever does a good deed, so its ruling is general. Al-Naqqash, al-Tha'labi, al-Qushayri and many other exegetes mentioned in the story of Ali, Fatimah and their servant girl a narration that is not sound and not established. Layth related it from Mujahid from Ibn Abbas, concerning the words of the Mighty and Majestic: *They fulfil the vow and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread. And they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive*. He said: "Al-Hasan and al-Husayn fell ill, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited them, as did the general public of the Arabs, and they said: 'O Abu al-Hasan—'" (Jabir al-Ju'fi related it from Qanbar, the freedman of Ali, who said: "Al-Hasan and al-Husayn fell ill until the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited them, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'O Abu al-Hasan—' The narration returns to the narration of Layth ibn Abi Sulaym—'If you would make a vow on behalf of your two sons for something.' And every vow that has no fulfilment is nothing." He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If my two sons recover, I will fast three days for Allah in thanks." A servant girl of theirs, a Nubian, said: "If my two masters recover, I will fast three days for Allah in thanks." Fatimah said the same. In the narration of al-Ju'fi, al-Hasan and al-Husayn said: "The same is upon us." The two boys were granted health, but there was nothing with the family of Muhammad, neither little nor much. So Ali went to Shim'un ibn Haria al-Khaybari, who was a Jew, and borrowed three *aṣwuʿ* of barley from him, and brought it, and placed it in a corner of the house. Fatimah stood up to a *ṣāʿ* of it, ground it, and baked it. Ali prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ), then came to the house, and the food was placed before him.

In the narration of al-Ju'fi: "The servant girl stood to a *ṣāʿ* of barley and baked from it five loaves, one for each of them. When their first fast ended, bread and coarsely ground salt were placed before them, when a needy man came to the door and said: 'Peace be upon you, people of the household of Muhammad'—in the narration of al-Ju'fi—'I am a needy man from the needy of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and by Allah I am hungry. Feed me, and Allah will feed you from the banquets of Paradise.' Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, heard him and composed, saying:"

*O Fatimah, possessor of virtue and certainty,*
*O daughter of the best of all people,*
*Do you not see the wretched needy man*
*Who has stood at the door, with a moaning cry?*
*He complains to Allah and humbles himself;*
*He complains to us, a hungry, grieved one.*
*Every person is a pledge for his earnings,*
*And the doer of good will be made manifest.*
*Our promised place is the Garden of 'Illiyyin,*
*Which Allah has forbidden to the miser,*
*And for the stingy there is a humiliating station*
*Where the Fire will hurl him down to Sijjin.*
*His drink is boiling water and pus;*
*Whoever does good will be well-nourished,*
*And will enter Paradise at any time.*

Then Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, composed, saying:

*Your command, O cousin, is obedience to me;*
*There is in me no baseness nor lowliness.*
*I rose early in making bread for him;*
*I feed him, and I care not for the hour.*
*I hope, when I satisfy the one in hunger,*
*To join the righteous and the community,*
*And to enter Paradise, for me is intercession.*

They fed him the food, and they remained their day and night without tasting anything but plain water. When the second day came, she stood to a *ṣāʿ*, ground it, and baked it, and Ali prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ), then came to the house, and the food was placed before them. Then an orphan stood at the door and said: "Peace be upon you, people of the household of Muhammad. An orphan from the children of the emigrants; my father was martyred on the day of al-ʿAqabah [as in the original]. Feed me, and Allah will feed you from the banquets of Paradise." Ali heard him and composed, saying:

*Fatimah, daughter of the noble master,*
*Daughter of a prophet, not of illegitimate birth,*
*Allah has brought the orphan to us;*
*Whoever shows mercy today will be shown mercy.*

And He will admit into Paradise whoever is safe (salim)... The eternal abode is forbidden to the base (la'im).

Not to cross the straight path (al-sirat al-mustaqim)... He slips into the Fire, down to the Blazing Hell.

His drink is pus and boiling water.

Then Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, recited:

I will feed him today, and I will not care,
and I will prefer Allah over my dependents.
They have gone hungry, and they are my cubs,
the youngest of them would be killed in battle.
Let him die a child, slain by treachery.
Woe to the killer who bears the burden,
whom the Fire will hurl down to the lowest depths,
with the shackle and the chains in his hands,
like a camel-foal that has outgrown its fetters.

So they gave him the food, and they stayed two days and two nights without tasting anything but plain water. When it was the third day, she got up to the remaining measure (sa') of grain, ground it and baked it. Ali prayed with the Prophet ﷺ, then came to the house, and the food was set before them. Suddenly a captive came and stood at the door and said: "Peace be upon you, people of the household of Muhammad! You take us captive and bind us, yet you do not feed us! Feed me, for I am a captive of Muhammad." Ali heard him and recited:

Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet Ahmad,
daughter of a prophet, a noble master,
He whom Allah named is Muhammad,
Allah adorned him with a graceful, beautiful beauty.
This is a captive of the guided Prophet,
heavy in his shackles, bound.
He complains to us of hunger, which has spread through him.
Whoever feeds him today will find it in tomorrow
with the Exalted, the One, the Unique.
What the planter plants, he will reap.
Give to him, no, do not let him sit idle.

Then Fatimah, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with her, recited:

Nothing remains of what came except one measure,
my hand has gone with the forearm.
By Allah, my two sons are hungry,
O Lord, do not leave them lost.
Their father is a doer of good for good,
who does kindness with innovation.
Broad of forearm, strong of stride,
and there is no veil on my head,
except a veil woven of leather thongs (ansa').

[[al-nasa' (with kasra): a thong braided in the shape of sandal straps, with which saddles are bound.]]

So they gave him the food, and they stayed three days and their nights, tasting nothing but plain water. When it was the fourth day, and Allah had fulfilled the vow, Ali took al-Hasan with his right hand and al-Husayn with his left, and went toward the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while they trembled like chicks from the intensity of hunger. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw them, he said: "O Abu al-Hasan, how grievous it is to me to see you like this. Come with us to my daughter Fatimah." They went to her, and she was in her prayer niche, her belly clung to her back, and her eyes had sunk from the intensity of hunger. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw her, and perceived the hunger in her face, he wept and said: "Alas, O Allah! The people of the household of Muhammad are dying of hunger!" Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and said: "Peace be upon you. Your Lord sends you His greetings, O Muhammad. Take this, joyfully, for your household." He said: "And what shall I take, O Jibril?" So he recited to him: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing mentioned?﴾ up to His words: ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive. "We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not want from you reward or gratitude."﴾

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah said in Nawadir al-Usul: This is an embellished, counterfeit hadith. Its transmitter has gone to extremes in it, so that it has become confused for the listeners. The ignorant person who knows this hadith bites his lips in regret that he is not of this description, and does not know that the doer of this act is blameworthy. Allah the Exalted has said in His revelation: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: That which is surplus﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], which is the excess beyond yourself and your dependents. Reports have come from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, transmitted by many chains, that [the best charity is that given out of sufficiency] and [begin with yourself, then with those you support]. Allah has made it obligatory upon husbands to provide maintenance for their wives and their children. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: [It is enough sin for a man that he neglects those he is responsible to feed.]

Would any intelligent person suppose that Ali was ignorant of this matter, so that he would exhaust young children, aged five or six, through three days and nights of hunger, until they writhed from hunger, their eyes sank because their stomachs were empty, and until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wept over the hardship they were in? Suppose he preferred this beggar over himself: would it have been permissible for him to compel his family to that? And suppose his family consented to it for Ali: would it have been permissible for him to compel his children to hunger for three days and their nights? Such a thing is only sold to foolish ignorant people. Allah forbid that attentive hearts should suspect Ali of such a thing. I wonder who memorized these verses every night about Ali and Fatimah, and each one's answer to the other, until he transmitted them to these narrators? This and similar reports are, in my view, among the tales of prisoners. I have been told that some people are confined in prisons for life, remaining without recourse, so they write reports for entertainment in evening gatherings and the like. Such reports are fabricated. When they reach the experts (al-jahabidhah), they reject them and expose their falsity. Every thing has a blight and a snare, and the blight and snare of religion are greater.

So they gave him the food, and they stayed three days and their nights, tasting nothing but plain water. The ignorant person who knows this hadith bites his lips in regret that he is not of this description, and does not know that the doer of this act is blameworthy. Allah the Exalted has said in His revelation: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: That which is surplus﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], which is the excess beyond yourself and your dependents. Reports have come from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, transmitted by many chains, that [the best charity is that given out of sufficiency] and [begin with yourself, then with those you support]. Allah has made it obligatory upon husbands to provide maintenance for their wives and their children. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: [It is enough sin for a man that he neglects those he is responsible to feed.]

Would any intelligent person suppose that Ali was ignorant of this matter, so that he would exhaust young children, aged five or six, through three days and nights of hunger, until they writhed from hunger, their eyes sank because their stomachs were empty, and until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wept over the hardship they were in? Suppose he preferred this beggar over himself: would it have been permissible for him to compel his family to that? And suppose his family consented to it for Ali: would it have been permissible for him to compel his children to hunger for three days and their nights? Such a thing is only sold to foolish ignorant people. Allah forbid that attentive hearts should suspect Ali of such a thing. I wonder who memorized these verses every night about Ali and Fatimah, and each one's answer to the other, until he transmitted them to these narrators? This and similar reports are, in my view, among the tales of prisoners. I have been told that some people are confined in prisons for life, remaining without recourse, so they write reports for entertainment in evening gatherings and the like. Such reports are fabricated. When they reach the experts (al-jahabidhah), they reject them and expose their falsity. Every thing has a blight and a snare, and the blight and snare of religion are greater.

The *nadhr* (vow) in its essential meaning is what the accountable person makes obligatory upon himself of some act. If you wish, you may define it thus: a vow is the accountable person making obligatory upon himself an act of obedience which would not have been obligatory for him had he not made it obligatory. Al-Kalbi said: "*Yūfūna bil-nadhr* means they complete the covenants, and the meaning is one." Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Then let them end their state of unkemptness and let them fulfil their vows﴾ [al-Hajj: 29], meaning the acts of their rites which they made obligatory upon themselves by entering the state of ihram for hajj. (Another reading: "having bequeathed.")

*And there became lowly to the nobles of Banu Lu'ayy a fire at al-Buwayrah that spreads.*

What the planter plants, he will reap.
Give to him, no, do not let him sit idle.

Then Fatimah, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with her, recited:

Nothing remains of what came except one measure,
my hand has gone with the forearm.
By Allah, my two sons are hungry,
O Lord, do not leave them lost.
Their father is a doer of good for good,
who does kindness with innovation.
Broad of forearm, strong of stride,
and there is no veil on my head,
except a veil woven of leather thongs (ansa').

[[al-nasa' (with kasra): a thong braided in the shape of sandal straps, with which saddles are bound.]]

So they gave him the food, and they stayed three days and their nights, tasting nothing but plain water. When it was the fourth day, and Allah had fulfilled the vow, Ali took al-Hasan with his right hand and al-Husayn with his left, and went toward the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, while they trembled like chicks from the intensity of hunger. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw them, he said: "O Abu al-Hasan, how grievous it is to me to see you like this. Come with us to my daughter Fatimah." They went to her, and she was in her prayer niche, her belly clung to her back, and her eyes had sunk from the intensity of hunger. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw her, and perceived the hunger in her face, he wept and said: "Alas, O Allah! The people of the household of Muhammad are dying of hunger!" Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and said: "Peace be upon you. Your Lord sends you His greetings, O Muhammad. Take this, joyfully, for your household." He said: "And what shall I take, O Jibril?" So he recited to him: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing mentioned?﴾ up to His words: ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive. "We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not want from you reward or gratitude."﴾

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu 'Abd Allah said in Nawadir al-Usul: This is an embellished, counterfeit hadith. Its transmitter has gone to extremes in it, so that it has become confused for the listeners. The ignorant person who knows this hadith bites his lips in regret that he is not of this description, and does not know that the doer of this act is blameworthy. Allah the Exalted has said in His revelation: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: That which is surplus﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], which is the excess beyond yourself and your dependents. Reports have come from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, transmitted by many chains, that [the best charity is that given out of sufficiency] and [begin with yourself, then with those you support]. Allah has made it obligatory upon husbands to provide maintenance for their wives and their children. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: [It is enough sin for a man that he neglects those he is responsible to feed.]

Would any intelligent person suppose that Ali was ignorant of this matter, so that he would exhaust young children, aged five or six, through three days and nights of hunger, until they writhed from hunger, their eyes sank because their stomachs were empty, and until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wept over the hardship they were in? Suppose he preferred this beggar over himself: would it have been permissible for him to compel his family to that? And suppose his family consented to it for Ali: would it have been permissible for him to compel his children to hunger for three days and their nights? Such a thing is only sold to foolish ignorant people. Allah forbid that attentive hearts should suspect Ali of such a thing. I wonder who memorized these verses every night about Ali and Fatimah, and each one's answer to the other, until he transmitted them to these narrators? This and similar reports are, in my view, among the tales of prisoners. I have been told that some people are confined in prisons for life, remaining without recourse, so they write reports for entertainment in evening gatherings and the like. Such reports are fabricated. When they reach the experts (al-jahabidhah), they reject them and expose their falsity. Every thing has a blight and a snare, and the blight and snare of religion are greater.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 76, verse 10–11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, we fear from our Lord a day [that is] austere and distressing.﴾ "ʿAbūsan" (austere) is an attribute of "yawm" (day): that is, a day on which faces frown (taʿbisu) because of its terror and severity. So the meaning is: "We fear a day possessing austerity." Ibn ʿAbbas said: the disbeliever frowns on that day until sweat flows from him like tar (qaṭrān). And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "al-ʿAbūs" is the constricted, and "al-Qamṭarīr" is the long. A poet said:

Severe, austere, and long-lasting

It was also said: "al-Qamṭarīr" means severe. The Arabs say: a day that is qamṭarīr, qumāṭir, and ʿaṣīb, with the same meaning. Al-Farrāʾ recited:

"O sons of our paternal uncles, do you remember our trials [inflicted] upon you when there was a qumāṭir day?"

with a damma on the qāf. And "iqmaṭarra" means it became intense. Al-Akhfash said: al-Qamṭarīr is the most intense and longest of days in calamity. A poet said:

"They fled when the dust of war was stirred up, and the austere, qumāṭir day pressed on with it."

Al-Kisaʾi said: it is said "iqmaṭarra al-yawm" and "izmaharra, iqmiṭrāran and izmihrāran," and it is al-qamṭarīr and al-zamharīr; and "yawm muqmaṭirr" when it is difficult and severe. Al-Hudhali said [[The verse is by Hudhayfa ibn Anas al-Hudhali; in the Diwan of the Hudhalis it reads:

"Sons of war, we were nursed with it, a qamṭarra [milk-bearing] she-camel, and whoever of us meets [it] meets a master trained [in war]."

"Arḍaʿnā" is in the passive. "Muqmaṭirra": from "aqmaṭarat al-nāqa" when she conceived. "Yalqa" is in the passive in both wordings. "Al-sayyid" among the Hudhayl is the lion. "Al-mudarrab" is the fierce one.]]:

"Sons of war, we were nursed for them with a qamṭarra [she-camel], and whoever of us meets that day flees."

Mujahid said: "al-ʿUbūs" is with the two lips, and "al-Qamṭarīr" is with the forehead and the two eyebrows; thus he made them attributes of the face changed by the severities of that day. Ibn al-Aʿrabi recited:

"He goes out hunting, returns broken, and at times frowns and scowls."

Abu ʿUbayda said: one says "rajulun qamṭarīr," meaning one who is contracted between the two eyes. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said "iqmaṭarrat al-nāqa" when she raised her tail, gathered her two sides (qutrayhā), and pushed her nose; he derived it from "al-qaṭr" and made the mīm an added letter. Asad ibn Nāʿiṣa said:

"I have endured wars every day, fierce in evil, austere in the morning."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Allah guarded them from the evil of that day﴾, that is, He repelled from them the evil of that day, its harm, its severity and its punishment; ﴿and gave them radiance﴾, that is, He granted and bestowed upon them when they met it, i.e., saw it, ﴿radiance﴾, that is, beauty, ﴿and joy﴾, that is, happiness. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: radiance in their faces and joy in their hearts. Regarding "al-naḍra" there are three views: the first is that it is whiteness and purity, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk; the second is beauty and splendour, said by Ibn Jubayr; the third is that it is the trace of blessing, said by Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 76, verse 12–14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He will reward them for what they endured with patience﴾, meaning patience over poverty. Al-Qurazi said: patience over fasting. ʿAtaʾ said: patience over hunger for three days, and these are the days of the vow. It was also said: for their patience in obedience to God, and their patience in refraining from disobedience to God and His prohibitions. The word "bi-ma" (with what) is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), and this is on the basis that the verse was revealed concerning all the righteous (al-abrar) and whoever does a good deed. Ibn ʿUmar narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about patience, and he said: "Patience is of four kinds: the first of them is patience at the first shock, patience in performing the obligatory duties, patience in avoiding the prohibitions of God, and patience in calamities."

(﴿Garden and silk﴾), that is, He will admit them to the Garden and clothe them in silk. It is said that it is called the silk of this world, and likewise that of the Hereafter, [and in it] is whatever favor God, Mighty and Majestic, wills. It has already been mentioned (see vol. 12, p. 19) that whoever wore silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter; rather, whoever is clothed in it in Paradise is clothed in it as a recompense for their having restrained themselves in this world from the garments which God forbade them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Reclining therein﴾, that is, in the Garden. The accusative of "muttaki'in" (reclining) is a circumstantial state (hal) from the hidden pronoun in "jazahum" (He rewarded them), and its governing element is "jaza" (rewarded); "sabaru" (they endured) does not govern it, because patience was in this world and reclining is in the Hereafter. Al-Farra' said: if you wish, you may make "muttaki'in" a follower (tabi'), as if he said: "He rewarded them with a Garden, reclining therein."

(﴿On couches﴾), that is, thrones (sururs) within canopies (hijal), and it has already been mentioned (see vol. 10, p. 398). Names have come from the Arabs that contain descriptions: one of them is "arikah," which is only a canopy upon a throne. Among them is "sajl," which is a bucket full of water; when it is empty it is not called a sajl, and likewise a "dhanub" is not called a dhanub until it is filled, and a "ka's" (cup) is not called a ka's until it is brimming with wine. Likewise, the tray upon which a gift is presented is called a "mihda" when it carries a gift, but when it is empty it is called "tabaq" or "khiwan." Dhu al-Rummah said:

Cheeks that have been worn lean by travel, until it is as though they touch the hard earth with the touch of couches [[al-mi'za': hard ground. He says: from the intensity of their need for sleep, they see the hard stony ground as if it were bedding on couches, which are thrones. It is narrated as "khududan" as an object of a verb in the line before it.]]

That is, the cushions upon the thrones.

(﴿They will see there neither sun﴾), that is, they will not see in the Garden intense heat like the heat of the sun, ﴿nor bitter cold﴾, that is, nor excessive cold. Al-A'sha said:

Pampered, a delicate girl, like the gazelle, she has not seen sun nor zamharir [[What is in the Diwan of al-A'sha, printed in Europe, reads: "mubtallat al-khalq mithl al-mahat..." etc.]]

It is narrated from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The Fire complained to its Lord, Mighty and Majestic, saying: 'O Lord, some of me has consumed other parts of me.' So He allowed it two breaths: a breath in winter and a breath in summer. Thus the intensity of the cold you find is from its zamharir, and the intensity of the heat you find in summer is from its samum." And from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, the air of Paradise is sajsaj: neither hot nor cold." The sajsaj is the extended shade that lies between the break of dawn and the rising of the sun. Murrah al-Hamdani said: the zamharir is the piercing cold. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: it is a thing like the heads of needles that descends from the sky in extreme cold. Ibn Mas'ud said: it is a kind of punishment, namely severe cold, such that when the people of the Fire are cast into it, they ask God to punish them with fire for a thousand years, which would be easier for them than the punishment of the zamharir for a single day. Abu al-Najm said:

Or I was a wind, I was zamharir

Tha'lab said: "al-zamharir" means the moon in the dialect of Tayy; their poet said:

And a night whose darkness has gathered thick, I crossed it while the zamharir had not shone

It is also narrated as "ma zahar," that is, the moon had not risen. So the meaning is: they will not see in it a sun like the sun of this world, nor a moon like the moon of this world; that is, they will be in a lasting light, with no night or day in it, because the light of day is by the sun and the light of night is by the moon. This meaning has already been fully discussed in Surah Maryam (see vol. 11, p. 127) at His saying: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: While the people of Paradise are in Paradise, they see a light which they think is the sun, which has risen and lit up Paradise with that light. They say: "Our Lord said: 'They will see there neither sun nor bitter cold'; so what is this light?" Ridwan says to them: "This is not a sun nor a moon, but rather this is Fatimah and ʿAli, who laughed, and the Gardens shone from the light of their laughter, and concerning them God, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Has there come upon man?﴾" And he recited:

I am the client of a youth, concerning whom was revealed "Has there come upon man,"
That is ʿAli al-Murtada, the cousin of the Chosen One.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And near them will be its shade﴾, that is, the shade of the trees in Paradise will be close to the righteous, so it will shade them, as an increase in their bliss, even though there is no sun or moon there, just as their combs will be of gold and silver, even though there is no dirt or disorder there. It is said that the trees in Paradise are a hundred years tall, and when the friend of God desires its fruit, it bends down until he can reach it. "Daniyah" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, in conjunction with "muttaki'in," as you say: "In the house is ʿAbd Allah reclining, and the curtains are let down over him." It was also said: it is in the accusative as a qualifier of the Garden, meaning: "He rewarded them with a near Garden," so it is an adjective for an omitted noun. It was also said: it is in the position of "They will see there neither sun nor bitter cold," and "they will see near"; it was also said: it is in the accusative by way of praise, meaning: "it has drawn near, near." This is said by al-Farra'. "Zilaluha" (its shades): "al-zilal" is in the nominative, governed by "daniyah." If it were read with "daniyah" in the nominative, with "al-zilal" as the subject and "daniyah" as the predicate, it would be permissible, and the clause would be in the position of a circumstantial state from the hidden pronoun in "jazahum," and this has indeed been read so. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah it is "wa-daniyan ʿalayhim," because of the preceding verb. In the codex of Ubayy it is "wa-dani," in the nominative, as a new sentence. ﴿And its clusters are made easy to reach﴾, that is, its fruits are made subservient to them, facilitated, that is, made easy to pick, so the one standing, sitting, or lying can take them; neither distance nor thorns prevent their hands from them, as said by Qatadah. Mujahid said: if one stands, it rises up for him; if he sits, it lowers itself to him; and if he lies down, it draws near to him so he eats from it. Also from him: the earth of Paradise is of silver, its dust is saffron, its perfume is pungent musk, the roots of its trees are gold and silver, its branches are pearls, emerald and ruby, and the fruit is beneath all of that. Whoever eats from it standing will not be harmed, whoever eats from it sitting will not be harmed, and whoever eats from it lying down will not be harmed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when one intends to take from its fruits, they bend down to him until he takes what he wants. The "tadhlil" of the clusters means the facilitating of reaching them. "Quṭūf" means fruits; the singular is "qitf" with a kasrah on the qaf, named so because it is picked (yuqtaf), just as the "jana" (fruit) is named so because it is gathered (yujna). "Tadhlilan" (made easy) is an emphasis for what was described as humbling, like His saying: ﴿And We sent it down in stages﴾ [al-Isra': 106] and ﴿And God spoke to Musa directly﴾ [al-Nisa': 164]. Al-Mawardi: It may be that the "tadhlil" of its clusters is that they emerge for them from their sheaths and are free of their stones for them. I say: this is far-fetched, for Ibn al-Mubarak narrated, saying: Sufyan informed us, from Hammad, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The palm trees of Paradise: their trunks are green emerald, their bases are red gold, their fronds are garments for the people of Paradise, from which are their cloaks and robes, and their fruit is like jugs and buckets, whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, and softer than butter, with no pit in it. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: It is said that "al-mudhallal" is one whom water has made pliant, that is, watered it. It is said that "al-mudhallal" is one whose shade a slight breeze moves because of its abundance. It is said that "al-mudhallal" is "the leveled," for the people of the Hijaz say: "dhallil nakhlaka," that is, level your palm. It is said that "al-mudhallal" is the near, easily reached, from their saying: "a wall dhalil," that is, low. Abu Ja'far said: These sayings we have related were mentioned by the scholars of language, and they cited them in the line of Imru' al-Qays:

And a shank like the reed-stalk of the watered, made pliant [[al-anbub: papyrus. al-saqy: watered palms. He likens the woman's shank to papyrus that has grown beneath palm trees, which shade it from the sun, and that is its most beautiful state. The beginning of the line: "And a slender waist like the jadil, shaped."]]

This was related from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. His saying "is named" means that it is mentioned by this name among the angels, the righteous and the people of Paradise. Salsabil is given tanwin (unless diptotic) because it is the end of a verse, like His saying: "the suspicions" [Al-Ahzab: 10] and "the way" [Al-Ahzab: 67].

Allah the Exalted says: "And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups." That is, the servants will go round among these righteous people when they desire drink, with vessels of silver. Ibn Abbas said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in Paradise except the names. What is in Paradise is more noble, higher and purer."

Then the golden vessels are not negated; rather the meaning is that they are given drink in vessels of silver, and they may also be given drink in vessels of gold. Allah the Exalted has said: "There will be circulated among them platters of gold and cups" [Az-Zukhruf: 71]. It was also said that mentioning silver draws attention to gold, like His saying: "Garments that protect you from the heat" [An-Nahl: 81], meaning and the cold, so mentioning one of them points to the other.

Al-Akwab (cups) are large pitchers that have neither handles nor spouts; the singular is kub. Adi said:

"Reclining, whose doors are knocked upon... a servant runs to him with the cup"

(Another reading: "tukhfaq" instead of "tuqra".)

This has already passed in commentary on Az-Zukhruf [see vol. 16, p. 111].

Allah the Exalted says: "Crystal-clear, crystal made of silver." That is, in the clearness of crystal and the whiteness of silver: its clarity is the clarity of glass, yet it is made of silver. It was also said: the ground of Paradise is of silver, and the vessels are made from the dust of the earth from which they come. This was related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There is nothing in Paradise except that you have been given in this world something similar to it, except the crystal of silver." And he said: "If you took silver from the silver of this world and beat it until it became as thin as a fly's wing, you would not see the water behind it; but the crystal of Paradise is like silver [i.e., in its whiteness] with the clarity of crystal."

Allah the Exalted says: "They have determined it with determination." The reading of the majority is with a fatha on the qaf and dal: that is, the cupbearers who circulate with them determined the measure for them. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said: they brought it according to their thirst, without excess or deficiency. Al-Kalbi said: that is more delicious and more appetising. The meaning is: the angels who circulate among them determined it. It is also related from Ibn Abbas: they measured it to the fill of the palm, neither more nor less, so that it would not harm them by heaviness or by excessive smallness. It was also said: the drinkers themselves determined measures for it according to what they desired and decided. Ubayd ibn Umayr, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Sirin read "qudirawha" with a damma on the qaf and a kasra on the dal, meaning that it was made for them according to the measure of their desire. Al-Mahdawi mentioned this reading from Ali and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and said: whoever reads "qaddarawha" it returns to the meaning of the other reading, and the original was "qudiru 'alayha" with the preposition dropped, and the meaning is "it was determined upon them." Sibawayh cited:

"I have sworn never to eat the grain of Iraq as long as I live, while the weevil eats the grain in the village."

He held that the meaning is "upon the grain of Iraq." It was also said: this determination means that the cups fly and dip according to the measure of the drinker's desire; this is the meaning of His saying: "They have determined it with determination," that is, it does not exceed the satisfaction nor fall short of it. The cups are inspired with knowledge of the measure of the desirer's satisfaction so that they dip by that measure. This view was mentioned by al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim in Nawadir al-Usul.

Allah the Exalted says: "And they will be given to drink therein a cup" which is wine in a vessel. "Its mixture will be ginger" (kana here is a connecting particle, meaning its mixture is ginger), or it was in God's judgment ginger. The Arabs found pleasure in drinks mixed with ginger because of its fine fragrance, since it sharpens the tongue and aids digestion; so they were encouraged toward the delights of the Hereafter by what they regarded as the utmost of bounty and sweetness. Al-Musayyab ibn Alas, describing a woman's mouth, said:

"As if the taste of ginger in it, when you tasted it, and the essence of wine..."

It is also narrated as "al-karm" (the vine). Another said:

"As if a bit of ginger had spent the night in her mouth, and honey poured out..."

Its like is the saying of al-A'sha:

"As if cloves and ginger had spent the night in her mouth, and honey poured out..."

Mujahid said: Zanjabil is the name of the spring from which the drink of the righteous is mixed. Qatadah likewise said: Zanjabil is the name of the spring from which those brought near drink purely, and it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise. It was also said: it is a spring in Paradise in which the taste of ginger is found. It was also said: there is in it the sense of a drink mixed with ginger, and the meaning is "as if there were ginger in it."

"A spring" is in apposition to "cup." It may also be in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "they will be given to drink a spring," or in the accusative by dropping the preposition, meaning "from a spring," as previously mentioned in His saying: "A spring from which the servants of Allah drink" [Al-Insan: 6].

"Therein" means in Paradise. "It is named Salsabil." Salsabil is the delicious drink; it is of the form fa'lalil, from salsala (to flow smoothly). The Arabs say: this is a smooth drink, salsal, salsal, and salsabil with the same meaning, that is, pleasant in taste and delicious. In al-Sihah: "The water flowed smoothly in the throat," and "I poured it into it"; water that is salsal and salsal is easy to enter the throat because of its sweetness and clarity, and salasil with a damma is similar. Al-Zajjaj said: Salsabil in the language is the name of what is at the extreme of smoothness, so it seems the spring was named by its attribute. It is related from Mujahid who said: "Salsabila: a piece of iron for the flow, flowing in their throats smoothly." Similar is related from Ibn Abbas: it is the iron of the flow. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi, and from it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit, may Allah be pleased with him:

"They are given to drink from the water of Barada... upon them, the Barada mixed with the smooth wine..."

﴿And there will go round among them youths of everlasting youth﴾. He clarifies who serves them with the vessels: that is, youths of everlasting youth serve them, for they are lighter in service. Then he said, "everlasting," meaning they remain as they are in youth, freshness and beauty, not aging or changing, and they stay the same age through the passage of time. It was also said: "everlasting" means they do not die. It was also said: "musawwarun, muqarratun," meaning adorned with earrings, and al-takhlid (the everlasting state) is adornment. This has already been discussed [See vol. 17, p. 202].

﴿And when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾. That is, you would think them, because of their beauty, their number and the purity of their complexions, to be pearls scattered across the floor of the assembly. Pearls, when scattered on a carpet, are more beautiful than when strung. It is related from al-Ma'mun that on the night Bourān, the daughter of al-Hasan ibn Sahl, was escorted to him, he was sitting on a carpet woven of gold, and the women of the caliph's household had scattered pearls over it. He looked at them scattered on that carpet, admired the sight, and said: "By Allah, how well Abu Nuwas described this, as if he had seen it, when he says:

*As if its large and small bubbles*
*Were pebbles of pearl on a ground of gold.*"

It was also said: he likened them to scattered pearls because they are swift in service, unlike the dark-eyed maidens (ḥūr 'īn), whom he likened to hidden, guarded pearls, because they are not degraded by service.

﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion﴾. Thamma is a locative adverbial of place, meaning "there, in Paradise." The governing element (al-'āmil) of thamma is the sense of "you see" (ra'ayta), that is: "and when you see with your eyes there." Al-Farra' said: in the sentence there is an implied "mā" (what), meaning "and when you see what is there," like His saying: ﴿Indeed, your bonds have been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94], meaning "what is between you." Al-Zajjaj said: "mā" is a relative pronoun joined to thamma according to what al-Farra' mentioned, and it is not permissible to drop the relative and leave out its clause; rather, ra'ayta is transitive in meaning to thamma, and the meaning is: "when you see with your eyes there," and by thamma he means Paradise. Al-Farra' also mentioned this. Al-Na'im (bliss) is all that one enjoys. Al-mulk al-kabīr (the great dominion) is the angels' seeking permission to enter, said al-Suddi and others. Al-Kalbi said: it is that a messenger comes from Allah with honours of clothing, food, drink and gifts to the friend of Allah while he is in his dwelling, and asks permission to enter upon him; that is the great dominion. Muqatil ibn Sulayman also said this. It was also said: the great dominion is that one of them has seventy chamberlains, one behind another. While the friend of Allah is in his delight and joy, a angel from Allah comes asking permission to enter, sent by Allah with a letter, a gift and a present from the Lord of the worlds, the like of which that friend has never seen in Paradise. So he says to the outermost chamberlain: "Ask permission for me from the friend of Allah, for I have with me a letter and a gift from the Lord of the worlds." That chamberlain says to the one next to him: "This is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, with a letter and a gift, seeking permission to enter upon the friend of Allah," and so he asks permission in the same way until it reaches the chamberlain who is nearest to the friend of Allah, and says to him: "O friend of Allah! This is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds seeking to enter upon you, with a letter and a present from the Lord of the worlds. Shall he be permitted?" He says: "Yes! Permit him." That chamberlain says to the one next to him: "Yes, permit him" (in other versions: "hasten to him"), and the one next to him says the same to the next, until it reaches the other chamberlain, who says: "Yes, O angel, you have been permitted," and he enters, greets him and says: "Peace sends you greetings, and this is a gift, and this is a letter to you from the Lord of the worlds." Then it is written on it: "From the Living who does not die, to the living who will die." He opens it, and in it is: "Peace upon My servant and friend, My mercy and My blessings. O My friend, is it not time for you to long for the sight of your Lord?" So longing overwhelms him, and he mounts the Buraq, and it flies with him, out of longing for more of the Knower of the unseen, and He gives him what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has never occurred to the heart of any human. Sufyan al-Thawri said: we have been told that the great dominion is the angels' greeting of them, and his evidence is His saying: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate: "Peace be upon you, for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final abode"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23–24]. It was also said: the great dominion is having crowns on their heads, as on the head of a king among kings. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: it means the dominion of creation (mulk al-takwīn), so that when they want something they say to it, "Be," and it is. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: a dominion not followed by ruin. And it is related in a report from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The great dominion is that the lowest of them in rank looks over his dominion a distance of two thousand years, seeing its farthest end as he sees its nearest." He said: "And the most excellent of them in rank is the one who looks upon the face of his Lord, may He be exalted, twice every day." Glory be to the Bestower of favours.

﴿Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade﴾. Nafi', Hamza and Ibn Muhaysin read ʿāliyahum with a sukun on the yā' (ʿāliyahum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it, taking into account the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Wathhab and others: "ʿāliyatuhum," and the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas: "Have you not seen the man who is wearing clothes, over which are finer clothes?" Al-Farra' said: it is in the nominative by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), and its predicate is "garments of sundus," and the active participle is intended to refer to the plural. According to al-Akhfash it is permissible for it to be in the singular, as an active participle that is fronted, with "garments" raised by it and serving as the predicate; the genitive construction in it is to be understood as separated, because it is not made definite, and it is begun with because it has been specified by the genitive. The rest read ʿāliyahum with the accusative. Al-Farra' said: it is like your saying "fawqahum" (above them), and the Arabs say "qawmuka dākhila al-dār" (your people inside the house), putting dākhil in the accusative as an adverb of place, because it is a locative. Al-Zajjaj rejected this and said: this is something we do not know in adverbs, and if it were an adverb it would not be permissible to pronounce the yā' with a sukun. Rather, it is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial state) relating to two things: the first is the hā' and mīm in His saying "yaṭūfu ʿalayhim" (go round among them), that is, upon the righteous, youths going round, with the righteous being elevated (ʿāliyan) by garments of sundus; that is, he goes round among them in this state. The second is that it is a ḥāl of the youths: that is, "when you see them you would think them scattered pearls" while the garments are high upon their bodies. Abu 'Ali said: the governing element of the ḥāl is either "laqqāhum naḍratan wa surūran" (He has granted them radiance and joy) or "jazāhum bi mā ṣabarū" (He has rewarded them for what they endured). He said: it is also permissible for it to be an adverb, and it is made into one. Al-Mahdawi said: it is also permissible for it to be an active participle functioning as an adverb, as in your saying "huwa nāḥiyatun min al-dār" (he is a side of the house); and because ʿāliyan has the sense of fawq (above), it is treated like it and made an adverb. Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim read khuḍrun (green) in the genitive as an adjective of sundus, and istabraq in the nominative as a conjunction with "al-thiyāb" (garments), and the meaning is: upon them are garments of sundus and istabraq. Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read khuḍrun in the nominative as an adjective of "thiyāb," and istabraq in the genitive as an adjective of sundus, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this for the soundness of its meaning, because khuḍr is best as an adjective of thiyāb, so it is nominative, and the best way to conjoin istabraq to sundus is as conjunction of kind upon kind; the meaning is: upon them are green garments of sundus and istabraq, that is, of these two kinds. Nafi' and Hafs read both in the nominative, with khuḍrun as an adjective of thiyāb, because both are in the plural form, and istabraq as a conjunction upon thiyāb. Al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read both in the genitive, and his saying "khuḍrun" is then an adjective of sundus; sundus is a noun of kind. Al-Akhfash permitted describing a noun of kind with a plural adjective, though he considered it objectionable, and you say: "ahlaka al-nās al-dīnār al-ṣufr wa al-dirham al-bīḍ" (the people destroyed the yellow dinars and the white dirhams), but it is far-fetched in speech. The meaning according to this reading is: upon them are garments of green sundus and garments of istabraq. All of them declined istabraq except Ibn Muhaysin, who gave it a fatḥa and did not decline it; so he read "wa istabraqa" in the accusative in place of the genitive, on the ground of prohibition of declension, since it is non-Arabic. This is an error, because it is an indefinite noun that admits the definite article; you say "al-istabraq," unless Ibn Muhaysin claims that it has become a proper name for this kind of garment. It is also read "wa ustabraqu" with a connected hamza and a fatḥa, on the ground that it is named after istaf'ala from al-barīq (gleam), and this is also not correct, because it is a well-known arabized word whose arabization is established, and its original form was istabrak. [In the original printed text it reads istabraq, which is an error, and the correction is from the Persian dictionary; in the Persian vocabularies and the explanation of the dictionary its origin is given as istabrah.] Sundus is what is fine of brocade, and istabraq is what is thick of it. [See vol. 10, p. 397 and vol. 17, p. 179.]

﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾. Wa ḥullū is conjoined to "yaṭūfu" (they go round). In Surat Fatir: ﴿they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾, and in Surat al-Hajj: ﴿they will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls﴾ [al-Hajj: 23]. It was said: the adornment of a man is silver and the adornment of a woman is gold. It was also said: at times they wear gold and at times they wear silver. It was also said: there are gathered on one of their arms two bracelets of gold, two of silver and two of pearls, so that the beauties of Paradise are combined for them; this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib. It was also said: that is, for each people is what their souls incline towards.

﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾. 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said concerning His saying: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾: when the people of Paradise set out for Paradise, they pass by a tree from beneath whose trunk two springs flow out. They drink from one of them, and the radiance of bliss flows over them, so their skins do not change and their hair never becomes disordered. Then they drink from the other, and what is in their bellies of impurities comes out. Then the keepers of Paradise meet them and say to them: ﴿Peace be upon you; you are good, so enter it to abide therein﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. Al-Nakha'i and Abu Qilaba said: when they drink it after eating, it purifies them, and what they have eaten and drunk becomes a sweat of musk, and their bellies become slender. Muqatil said: it is from a spring of water at the gate of Paradise, gushing from the trunk of a tree; whoever drinks from it, Allah removes from his heart whatever rancour, deceit and envy was there, and from his inside whatever harm and filth. This is the meaning of what is related from 'Ali, except that according to Muqatil's view it is a single spring; on this view, fa'ūl is for intensification, and there is no proof in it for the Hanafi that it means "pure" (ṭāhir). Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Furqan [See vol. 13, p. 39], and praise be to Allah. Tayyib al-Jammal said: I prayed behind Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah the 'atama (night) prayer, and he recited ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ and began moving his lips and mouth as if sucking something; when he finished, he was asked: "Do you drink or recite?" He said: "By Allah, if I did not find its pleasure in its recitation like its pleasure in drinking it, I would not have recited it."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 76, verse 19–22 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this has been for you a reward﴾, meaning: it will be said to them, "This is only a reward for you," that is, a recompense (thawab). ﴿And your effort has been appreciated﴾, meaning: your deeds have been appreciated by Allah. His appreciation (shukr) for the servant is the acceptance of his obedience, his praise of him, and his granting him recompense. Sa'id reported from Qatadah that he said: "He forgave them their sins and appreciated their good deeds." Mujahid said: "Mashkuran means accepted (maqbulan)." The meanings are close, for when He, glorified is He, accepts the deed, He appreciates it, and when He appreciates it, He rewards it abundantly, since He, glorified is He, is Possessor of great bounty.

It is narrated from Ibn Umar that a black man said: "O Messenger of Allah! You have been favoured over us with forms, colours and prophethood. What do you think: if I believe in what you believe in, and act by what you act, will I be with you in Paradise?" It was also said: that is, for each people is what their souls incline towards.

﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾. 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said concerning His saying: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾: when the people of Paradise set out for Paradise, they pass by a tree from beneath whose trunk two springs flow out. They drink from one of them, and the radiance of bliss flows over them, so their skins do not change and their hair never becomes disordered. Then they drink from the other, and what is in their bellies of impurities comes out. Then the keepers of Paradise meet them and say to them: ﴿Peace be upon you; you are good, so enter it to abide therein﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. Al-Nakha'i and Abu Qilaba said: when they drink it after eating, it purifies them, and what they have eaten and drunk becomes a sweat of musk, and their bellies become slender. Muqatil said: it is from a spring of water at the gate of Paradise, gushing from the trunk of a tree; whoever drinks from it, Allah removes from his heart whatever rancour, deceit and envy was there, and from his inside whatever harm and filth. This is the meaning of what is related from 'Ali, except that according to Muqatil's view it is a single spring; on this view, fa'ūl is for intensification, and there is no proof in it for the Hanafi that it means "pure" (ṭāhir). Its explanation has already passed in Surat al-Furqan [See vol. 13, p. 39], and praise be to Allah. Tayyib al-Jammal said: I prayed behind Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah the 'atama (night) prayer, and he recited ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ and began moving his lips and mouth as if sucking something; when he finished, he was asked: "Do you drink or recite?" He said: "By Allah, if I did not find its pleasure in its recitation like its pleasure in drinking it, I would not have recited it."

What do you think: if I believe in what you believe in, and act by what you act, will I be with you in Paradise?" Then a blessing from the blessings of Allah will come and nearly exhaust all of that, unless Allah shows kindness to him by His mercy.] He said: Then there was revealed: ﴿Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and a great kingdom﴾. Ibn Umar said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lowering him into his grave and saying: ﴿Indeed, this has been for you a reward, and your effort has been appreciated﴾."
