﴿And there will go round among them youths of everlasting youth﴾. He clarifies who serves them with the vessels: that is, youths of everlasting youth serve them, for they are lighter in service. Then he said, "everlasting," meaning they remain as they are in youth, freshness and beauty, not aging or changing, and they stay the same age through the passage of time. It was also said: "everlasting" means they do not die. It was also said: "musawwarun, muqarratun," meaning adorned with earrings, and al-takhlid (the everlasting state) is adornment. This has already been discussed [See vol. 17, p. 202].

﴿And when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾. That is, you would think them, because of their beauty, their number and the purity of their complexions, to be pearls scattered across the floor of the assembly. Pearls, when scattered on a carpet, are more beautiful than when strung. It is related from al-Ma'mun that on the night Bourān, the daughter of al-Hasan ibn Sahl, was escorted to him, he was sitting on a carpet woven of gold, and the women of the caliph's household had scattered pearls over it. He looked at them scattered on that carpet, admired the sight, and said: "By Allah, how well Abu Nuwas described this, as if he had seen it, when he says:

*As if its large and small bubbles*
*Were pebbles of pearl on a ground of gold.*"

It was also said: he likened them to scattered pearls because they are swift in service, unlike the dark-eyed maidens (ḥūr 'īn), whom he likened to hidden, guarded pearls, because they are not degraded by service.

﴿And when you look there, you will see bliss and a great dominion﴾. Thamma is a locative adverbial of place, meaning "there, in Paradise." The governing element (al-'āmil) of thamma is the sense of "you see" (ra'ayta), that is: "and when you see with your eyes there." Al-Farra' said: in the sentence there is an implied "mā" (what), meaning "and when you see what is there," like His saying: ﴿Indeed, your bonds have been severed﴾ [al-An'am: 94], meaning "what is between you." Al-Zajjaj said: "mā" is a relative pronoun joined to thamma according to what al-Farra' mentioned, and it is not permissible to drop the relative and leave out its clause; rather, ra'ayta is transitive in meaning to thamma, and the meaning is: "when you see with your eyes there," and by thamma he means Paradise. Al-Farra' also mentioned this. Al-Na'im (bliss) is all that one enjoys. Al-mulk al-kabīr (the great dominion) is the angels' seeking permission to enter, said al-Suddi and others. Al-Kalbi said: it is that a messenger comes from Allah with honours of clothing, food, drink and gifts to the friend of Allah while he is in his dwelling, and asks permission to enter upon him; that is the great dominion. Muqatil ibn Sulayman also said this. It was also said: the great dominion is that one of them has seventy chamberlains, one behind another. While the friend of Allah is in his delight and joy, a angel from Allah comes asking permission to enter, sent by Allah with a letter, a gift and a present from the Lord of the worlds, the like of which that friend has never seen in Paradise. So he says to the outermost chamberlain: "Ask permission for me from the friend of Allah, for I have with me a letter and a gift from the Lord of the worlds." That chamberlain says to the one next to him: "This is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, with a letter and a gift, seeking permission to enter upon the friend of Allah," and so he asks permission in the same way until it reaches the chamberlain who is nearest to the friend of Allah, and says to him: "O friend of Allah! This is a messenger from the Lord of the worlds seeking to enter upon you, with a letter and a present from the Lord of the worlds. Shall he be permitted?" He says: "Yes! Permit him." That chamberlain says to the one next to him: "Yes, permit him" (in other versions: "hasten to him"), and the one next to him says the same to the next, until it reaches the other chamberlain, who says: "Yes, O angel, you have been permitted," and he enters, greets him and says: "Peace sends you greetings, and this is a gift, and this is a letter to you from the Lord of the worlds." Then it is written on it: "From the Living who does not die, to the living who will die." He opens it, and in it is: "Peace upon My servant and friend, My mercy and My blessings. It was also said: the great dominion is having crowns on their heads, as on the head of a king among kings. Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: it means the dominion of creation (mulk al-takwīn), so that when they want something they say to it, "Be," and it is. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: a dominion not followed by ruin. ﴿Upon them will be garments of fine green silk and brocade﴾. Nafi', Hamza and Ibn Muhaysin read ʿāliyahum with a sukun on the yā' (ʿāliyahum), and Abu 'Ubayd preferred it, taking into account the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Wathhab and others: "ʿāliyatuhum," and the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas: "Have you not seen the man who is wearing clothes, over which are finer clothes?" Nafi' and Hafs read both in the nominative, with khuḍrun as an adjective of thiyāb, because both are in the plural form, and istabraq as a conjunction upon thiyāb. Al-A'mash, Ibn Wathhab, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read both in the genitive, and his saying "khuḍrun" is then an adjective of sundus; sundus is a noun of kind. Al-Akhfash permitted describing a noun of kind with a plural adjective, though he considered it objectionable, and you say: "ahlaka al-nās al-dīnār al-ṣufr wa al-dirham al-bīḍ" (the people destroyed the yellow dinars and the white dirhams), but it is far-fetched in speech. The meaning according to this reading is: upon them are garments of green sundus and garments of istabraq. All of them declined istabraq except Ibn Muhaysin, who gave it a fatḥa and did not decline it; so he read "wa istabraqa" in the accusative in place of the genitive, on the ground of prohibition of declension, since it is non-Arabic. This is an error, because it is an indefinite noun that admits the definite article; you say "al-istabraq," unless Ibn Muhaysin claims that it has become a proper name for this kind of garment. It is also read "wa ustabraqu" with a connected hamza and a fatḥa, on the ground that it is named after istaf'ala from al-barīq (gleam), and this is also not correct, because it is a well-known arabized word whose arabization is established, and its original form was istabrak. [In the original printed text it reads istabraq, which is an error, and the correction is from the Persian dictionary; in the Persian vocabularies and the explanation of the dictionary its origin is given as istabrah.] Sundus is what is fine of brocade, and istabraq is what is thick of it. [See vol. 10, p. 397 and vol. 17, p. 179.]

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 76, verse 23–26:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down to you the Quran, sending it down progressively﴾. [It means:] You did not invent it, nor did you bring it from yourself or from your own thought, as the polytheists claim. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He, glorified is He, mentioned the categories of promise and threat, He clarified that this Book contains what people are in need of, so it is neither magic, nor soothsaying, nor poetry, and that it is the truth. Ibn 'Abbas said: the Quran was sent down in installments, verse after verse, and was not sent down all at once; therefore He said "sent down" (nazzalna). The discussion of this has already been explained [see vol. 13, p. 29], and praise be to God.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord﴾, that is, for the decree of your Lord. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Be patient with the harm of the polytheists; thus has I decreed." Then it was abrogated (nusikha) by the verse of fighting. It was also said: be patient regarding what has been imposed upon you of acts of obedience, or wait for God's judgment, since He promised you that He would grant you victory over them, and do not hasten, for it will certainly come to pass. ﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever﴾: that is, do not obey any one of them who is sinful, or any disbeliever; that is, do not obey the disbelievers. Ma'mar narrated from Qatadah, who said: Abu Jahl said, "If I see Muhammad praying, I will surely step on his neck." So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever﴾. It is also said that it was revealed concerning 'Utba ibn Rabi'a and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) offering him wealth and marriage on condition that he leave off mentioning prophethood; so concerning the two of them the verse was revealed: ﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever﴾. Muqatil said: the one who offered marriage was 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, who said, "My daughters are among the most beautiful women of Quraysh, so I will marry you my daughter without a dowry, and turn back from this matter." Al-Walid said, "If you did what you did for the sake of wealth, I will give you wealth until you are content, and turn back from this matter," and so it was revealed. Then it was said: the "aw" (or) in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿sinner or disbeliever﴾ is more emphatic than "wa" (and), because if you say, "Do not obey Zayd and 'Amr," and he obeys one of them, he is not disobedient, since you ordered him not to obey both; but when he says, "Do not obey from among them any sinner or disbeliever," the "aw" indicates that each of them is deserving of being disobeyed, just as when you say, "Do not oppose al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," or "Follow al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," you have said that these two are deserving of being followed and each one of them is deserving of being followed. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: "aw" here has the function of "la" (not), as if he said: "nor a disbeliever." The poet said:

"No grief of a bereaved mother is like what I have felt, nor the grief of a distraught she-camel whose young calf (rabi') has strayed,
Or the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel on the day the pilgrims gathered and dispersed."

[Note: al-'ajul among women and camels is the distraught one who has lost her offspring; it was so called for her haste in coming and going out of anguish, and here it means the she-camel. Al-Rabi' (as in Kamuqd) is the foal born in spring.]

He meant: "nor the grief of an old man." It was also said: the sinner (al-athim) is the hypocrite, and the disbeliever (al-kafur) is the one who openly displays disbelief; that is, do not obey from among them any sinner or any disbeliever. This is close to the saying of al-Farra'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And mention the name of your Lord morning and evening﴾, that is, pray to your Lord at the beginning and end of the day: at its beginning is the dawn prayer, and at its end the noon and afternoon prayers. ﴿And prostrate to Him during part of the night﴾ refers to the sunset prayer and the late night prayer ('isha' al-akhirah). ﴿And glorify Him through the long night﴾ refers to voluntary prayer during the night; this was said by Ibn Habib. Ibn 'Abbas and Sufyan said: every glorification (tasbih) in the Quran is a prayer. It was also said: it is general remembrance of God, whether in prayer or outside it. Ibn Zayd and others said: His saying, "and glorify Him through the long night," has been abrogated by the five prayers. It was also said: it is recommended. It was also said: it is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). The discussion of a similar matter has already been given in surah al-Muzzammil [see p. 38 of this part]. The saying of Ibn Habib is good. The plural of al-asil is al-asa'il and al-usul, like your saying safa'in and sufun; the poet said:

"Nor is anything more beautiful than it when the evening (al-usul) draws near."

And another said, using al-asa'il, which is a plural of a plural:

"By my life, you are indeed the house whose people I honor, and I sit in its shade in the evenings (al-asa'il)."

This has already been discussed fully at the end of surah al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 355]. The particle "min" (from) entered upon the adverbial noun to indicate partiality, just as it entered upon the object in His saying: ﴿that He may forgive you some of your sins﴾.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 76, verses 29–31:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder; so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.﴾ "This" refers to the surah, "a reminder" means an admonition. "Whoever wills may take a way" means a path that leads to His obedience and the pursuit of His good pleasure. It was also said: "a way" means a means. It was also said: a direction and a path to Paradise [[In manuscripts B, Z, T: "to goodness."]]. The meaning is one. ﴿And you do not will﴾ means obedience, steadfastness, and taking the way to God, ﴿except that God wills﴾. He thus informed that the matter rests with Him, Glorified is He, and not with them, and that no one's will takes effect or precedes His, except that His will precedes theirs.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "wa ma yashaoon" with the *ya'* (third person), as a report about them. The rest read it with the *ta'* (second person), as addressed to God, Glorified is He.

It was said that the first verse is abrogated (*mansukha*) by the second (naskh, abrogation). The more likely view is that it is not abrogation; rather, it clarifies that this cannot happen except by His will.

Al-Farra' said: ﴿And you do not will except that God wills﴾ is the response to His saying ﴿whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾. Then He informed them that the matter is not in their hands, so He said: ﴿And you do not will that way except that God wills for you.﴾ ﴿Indeed God is ever Knowing of your deeds, Wise in His command and His prohibition to you.﴾ This has been discussed in other places.

﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾, meaning He admits him into Paradise, showing mercy to him. ﴿And the wrongdoers﴾, meaning He punishes the wrongdoers. Their accusative case (*nasb*) is by the implied verb "He punishes" (*yu'adhdhibu*).

Al-Zajjaj said: "*al-zalimin*" is in the accusative because what precedes it is in the accusative, meaning: He admits whom He wills into His mercy and punishes the wrongdoers, i.e., the polytheists. And "He has prepared for them" serves as an explanation of this implied verb, as the poet said:

*Aṣbaḥtu lā aḥmilu al-silāḥa wa lā*
*amliku ra's al-ba'īri in nafara*

*Wa al-dhi'ba akhshāhu in marartu bihi*
*waḥdī wa akhshā al-riyāḥa wal-maṭara*

That is: "I fear the wolf, I fear it if I pass by it alone, and I fear the winds and the rain."

Al-Zajjaj said: The preferred reading is the accusative, though the nominative is permissible. You say: "I gave Zayd and 'Amr, I have prepared goodness for him," so the accusative is preferred, meaning: "and I did good to 'Amr" or "I do good to 'Amr." As for His saying in "Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf" (al-Shura: 8), ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy, and the wrongdoers﴾, it is in the nominative because no verb follows it that governs it in meaning, so the coordination with the accusative before it is not permitted, and it is nominative by being the subject of a nominal sentence. Here, His saying "He has prepared for them a punishment" indicates "and He punishes," so the accusative is permitted.

Aban ibn 'Uthman read "wa al-zalimuna" in the nominative, as the subject, with the predicate being "He has prepared for them."

﴿A painful punishment﴾, meaning causing pain and agony. This has already been discussed in Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 198]] and elsewhere, and praise belongs to God.

*The surah is concluded.*
